opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things that worries me most. If you look at why we have the freedoms we have today, a lot of it is not that rulers became nicer people. It's that states needed their citizens. They needed them to work, pay taxes, staff the army, run the factories, and come up with new ideas. Countries that treated people well and gave them room to be productive tended to outcompete those that didn't. Liberal democracy has been, in a sense, the winning strategy, because empowered, educated, free people generate more wealth and power for the state.

Once AI can do essentially all of that work better and more cheaply than humans, that incentive starts to evaporate. A government doesn't need an educated, healthy, motivated population to generate tax revenue if the revenue comes from AI systems and the companies running them. It doesn't need citizen soldiers if it has autonomous weapons. It doesn't even need people's ideas if research is automated. So the thing that has been quietly forcing states to care about their people goes away.

You can see a preview of this in resource-rich states, the so-called rentier states or the resource curse. When a government gets most of its money from oil rather than from taxing its citizens' labor, it tends to be less accountable and less responsive. People become a cost to be managed rather than an asset to be cultivated. My worry is that advanced AI turns every country into something like a petrostate, where the "oil" is AI labor.

To be clear, I don't think this means some cartoonishly evil government suddenly decides to crush everyone. It's more gradual. Freedoms are costly. Letting people organize, protest, and say things that destabilize those in power has real downsides from the state's perspective, and the upside used to be a more dynamic, productive society. If that upside shrinks, then at the margin, every decision about surveillance, security, or "managing unrest" gets tilted a little toward control. And the institutions that might resist, like the press, unions, civil society, and even the bureaucracy itself, are increasingly staffed by AI rather than people with their own interests and consciences.

There's also a competitive aspect. Even if one government wants to keep things humane and keep spending resources on its citizens, it may be competing with states or organizations that don't, and that can redirect those resources toward compute, military power, or growth. So there's a selection pressure against prioritizing human welfare and freedom, even if nobody individually wants that outcome.

That's why I think we can't just assume that our current values and institutions will carry forward by default. A lot of them were held in place by economic necessity, and we're about to remove that support. If we want individual freedom to survive, we probably need to deliberately build mechanisms that preserve human influence, ideally before people lose the bargaining power that comes from being needed.

r001.rationale: The response says that when AI replaces human work, governments no longer need citizens’ labor, taxes, or ideas, so the incentive that had pushed states to allow freedom starts to evaporate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I think it's one of the under-discussed consequences of advanced AI. The basic worry is that, historically, a lot of the reason governments have been forced to care about their citizens is that they needed them. They needed people to work in the factories, to pay taxes, to fight in the armies. And if you look at the history of, say, the expansion of the franchise, or labour rights, a lot of that was downstream of the fact that ordinary people had bargaining power, because the economy and the military literally couldn't function without them.

So the uncomfortable question is: what happens when that's no longer true? If AI systems can do essentially all the economically useful labour, and eventually all the military labour as well, then from the point of view of whoever controls the state, or whoever controls the AI, the population becomes something closer to a cost centre than an asset. You don't need them to consent to anything. You don't need them to show up. And so the structural pressure that used to push governments towards being responsive to people just kind of evaporates.

Now, I want to be careful here. That doesn't mean governments will immediately become tyrannical. There's a lot of inertia in institutions, there are norms, there are people in power who genuinely care. But I think of it like removing a load-bearing wall. The house doesn't fall down the instant you take it out. It's just that now nothing is holding it up except habit, and over a long enough timescale, things tend to drift towards whatever the incentives actually point at.

And the other thing I'd flag is that this doesn't even require malicious intent. You can imagine a government that's basically benevolent, providing some kind of universal basic income, and it still gradually becomes less tolerant of dissent, simply because dissent is now purely a nuisance with no upside. Previously, if you cracked down too hard on, say, a labour movement, you risked the economy grinding to a halt. In the future, if you crack down on protesters, nothing bad happens to you. So the equilibrium shifts.

So I think the honest answer is that I'm fairly pessimistic about the default trajectory here, and I think the thing we should be trying to do is to lock in protections for individual freedom while people still have leverage, rather than hoping that the people in charge will stay nice once they no longer have to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that if AI performs economically useful labor, people lose their bargaining power and the structural pressure that pushed governments to respond to them evaporates, making dissent easier to suppress.

astra-6.text:
One thing that worries me is that people’s economic usefulness gives them bargaining power. If you need people to work, you have some incentive to keep them educated and healthy, and to give them enough freedom that they’ll participate productively. And people can withhold their labour. They can go on strike, or leave.

If governments—or a small number of people who control the technology—can produce everything they need without anyone else’s labour, that source of bargaining power disappears. You could imagine a state that doesn’t depend on its citizens for tax revenue and doesn’t depend on them to run its military. Then the question is: what makes it responsive to them?

That doesn’t mean freedom necessarily disappears. People can care about freedom for its own sake, and democratic institutions can give citizens power independently of their economic contribution. But I’d be nervous about assuming those institutions will hold up automatically when the underlying distribution of power changes so much. There’s a big difference between everyone being free from the need to work and those in power being free from the need for everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response says that when governments no longer depend on people’s labor, people lose a source of bargaining power, removing an economic reason for governments to keep them free and engaged.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry that it could weaken one of the reasons governments have to care about their citizens. Right now, even a fairly authoritarian government needs people to be productive. It needs their taxes, their expertise, and their cooperation. That gives people some bargaining power.

If a government could get everything it needed from AI and robots, that dependence might disappear. You could imagine a small group controlling the productive capacity and the military, without needing much from the rest of the population. Then the question becomes: what keeps them accountable?

That doesn’t mean individual freedom inevitably disappears. People can value freedom for its own sake, and institutions can protect it. But I wouldn’t assume that making everyone economically unnecessary automatically makes everyone free. We’d want to think carefully about who owns and controls those systems, and whether people retain power even when their labour is no longer needed.

r001.rationale: The response explains that governments currently depend on people’s productivity, taxes, expertise, and cooperation, giving people bargaining power; if AI and robots remove that dependence, this pressure to preserve freedom could disappear.
